subChunks.title: Entities, Value Objects & Aggregates

storyBeats.text: You have reached the highest vault of the Academy — Expert tier. Here, spells don't just run; they model entire worlds.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Before you write a single class, ask: what IS this thing in the real world? Is it defined by its identity, or by its values? That question determines everything.

storyBeats.label: Value Object equality

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an immutable Address value object with fields street, city, postcode. Override equals and hashCode. Print whether two identical addresses are equal.
guidedPractice.hint: Override equals() to compare all three fields. Use Objects.equals() or compare each field individually.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between an Entity and a Value Object. Why does immutability matter for Value Objects?

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an Entity from a Value Object in DDD?
options: Entities have unique identity; Value Objects are defined by attributes
Entities are immutable; Value Objects are mutable
Entities are simpler; Value Objects are complex
Value Objects have IDs; Entities do not
questions.answer: Entities have unique identity; Value Objects are defined by attributes
questions.explanation: Entity equality is based on ID. Value Object equality is based on all its attribute values.

questions.prompt: An Aggregate Root enforces which key responsibility?
options: Maintains all business invariants for the aggregate
Stores the aggregate in the database
questions.answer: Maintains all business invariants for the aggregate
questions.explanation: The Aggregate Root is the single entry point — all mutations go through it so invariants are always checked.

questions.prompt: Value Objects should be immutable — once created, their state never changes.
questions.explanation: Immutability makes Value Objects safe to share and easy to reason about.

subChunks.title: Bounded Contexts & Ubiquitous Language

storyBeats.text: The Council of Archmages governs different domains — Finance, Combat, Alchemy. Each has its own lexicon. 'Reagent' means gold coin in Finance but a potion ingredient in Alchemy.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Never let one context's model pollute another. Use an Anti-Corruption Layer like a diplomatic translator — it speaks both languages so your core models don't have to.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Sketch two classes: SalesOrder (has customerId, totalAmount) and ShippingOrder (has orderId, deliveryAddress). Write a translate method that creates a ShippingOrder from a SalesOrder.
guidedPractice.hint: translate() takes a SalesOrder and an address String, returns new ShippingOrder(so.orderId, address).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Bounded Contexts and Ubiquitous Language. Why can the same word have different meanings in different contexts?

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an Anti-Corruption Layer?
options: Translates between two domain models without polluting either
questions.answer: Translates between two domain models without polluting either
questions.explanation: An ACL acts as a translator at context boundaries, keeping each model clean.

questions.prompt: Two microservices both have a `Product` class but with different fields. How should they communicate?
options: Use a published language (shared event/DTO format) or Anti-Corruption Layer in each service to translate between their internal models
Share the Product class via a common library
questions.answer: Use a published language (shared event/DTO format) or Anti-Corruption Layer in each service to translate between their internal models
questions.explanation: Each service should own its model; integration happens at boundaries via translation, not shared classes.

subChunks.title: Domain Services & Application Services

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A domain service holds wisdom about the domain — it knows the rules. An application service is the logistics officer — it fetches resources and delegates work. Keep them apart.
Confusing the two is a common mistake. An application service that contains business logic is a sign the logic belongs in the domain.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a PricingService domain service that calculates the total price of an order: base price × quantity, minus 10% discount if quantity ≥ 10.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What is the difference between a Domain Service and an Application Service? Give an example of each.

questions.prompt: Where should a Domain Service live in the architecture?
options: In the domain layer, containing pure business logic
In the infrastructure layer, accessing the database
In the presentation layer, handling HTTP requests
In the application layer, alongside controllers
questions.answer: In the domain layer, containing pure business logic
questions.explanation: Domain Services contain domain logic and must not depend on infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Application Services should contain core business rules and calculations.
questions.explanation: Application Services orchestrate — they should be thin. Business rules belong in Entities or Domain Services.

subChunks.title: Repositories & Hexagonal Architecture

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The hexagon keeps your domain pure. Think of it as a spell that works regardless of which grimoire it was cast from. Swap PostgreSQL for MongoDB — the domain never knows.
The key rule: all dependencies point inward toward the domain. Frameworks depend on you, not the other way round.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Define an interface ProductRepository with save(String name, double price) and findByName(String name). Implement it with an in-memory HashMap. Save two products and retrieve one by name.
guidedPractice.hint: InMemoryProductRepository uses Map<String, Double>. save puts the price, findByName gets it.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Hexagonal Architecture. Why are Ports and Adapters defined in separate layers?

questions.prompt: In Hexagonal Architecture, where do dependencies point?
questions.explanation: All dependencies point inward. Adapters depend on port interfaces; the domain depends on nothing external.

options: The domain entity imports a Spring JPA interface — the domain depends on infrastructure. The repository port should be an interface defined in the domain layer.
JpaRepository cannot be injected this way
questions.answer: The domain entity imports a Spring JPA interface — the domain depends on infrastructure. The repository port should be an interface defined in the domain layer.
questions.explanation: Domain objects must never import framework or infrastructure classes. The dependency inversion principle keeps the domain clean.
